title: Processes and threads
scopeHtml:
Scope: process vs program, PCB and states, fork/exec, copy-on-write, threads and thread models, context switch cost.

Scope: process vs program, PCB and states, fork/exec, copy-on-write, threads and thread models, context switch cost.

notes.title: Process vs program
notes.html:
A program is a file on disk (instructions). A process is a program that is running, with its own memory, open files and state. Run the same program twice and you get two processes.

A process owns:

  • A private virtual address space: code, data, heap, stack, mapped libraries.
  • Open file descriptors (0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr, then sockets, files).
  • Credentials (user ID, group ID), current directory, environment variables, signal handlers.
  • One or more threads of execution.

You can see it all in /proc:

$ ls /proc/$$           # $$ = this shell
cmdline  cwd  environ  exe  fd  maps  smaps  stat  status  task ...
$ grep -E 'Name|State|Pid|PPid|Threads|VmRSS' /proc/$$/status
Name:   bash
State:  S (sleeping)
Pid:    3120
PPid:   3101
VmRSS:  4120 kB
Threads:        1

Worked example. A Postgres server forks one backend process per client connection, each about 5 to 10 MB of private memory. 500 connections cost 2.5 to 5 GB before any query runs, which is why PgBouncer pooling is standard past a few hundred connections.

Industry examples. Chrome runs one process per tab for isolation (a crash or exploit stays inside it). Nginx uses a few worker processes, each handling thousands of connections with epoll. Postgres is process-per-connection; MySQL is thread-per-connection.

Everyday analogy. A recipe (program) versus a cook actually cooking it in their own kitchen (process). Two cooks on one recipe are two processes.

Common interview traps.

  • Using "process" and "program" as synonyms.
  • Forgetting that the isolation boundary is the process: one process cannot read another's memory without OS help.

notes.title: Process states and the PCB
notes.html:
The kernel tracks each process in a record called the Process Control Block (PCB). In Linux it is struct task_struct (a few KB). It holds: PID, state, saved CPU registers, page table pointer, open files table, signal state, scheduling info (priority, vruntime), parent and children, cgroup and namespace links.

States (what ps and top show in the S column):

  • R running or runnable (on a CPU or in the run queue)
  • S sleeping, interruptible (waiting for an event; can take signals)
  • D uninterruptible sleep (usually waiting on disk or NFS; cannot be killed)
  • T stopped (Ctrl-Z or debugger)
  • Z zombie (finished, parent has not collected exit code)
$ ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,wchan:20,cmd | head
  PID  PPID STAT WCHAN                CMD
    1     0 Ss   do_epoll_wait        /sbin/init
 2210  2188 D    io_schedule          dd if=/dev/sda of=/dev/null
 2301  1200 Z    -                    [worker] <defunct>

Production incident patterns.

  • Many D processes and a load average of 50 on an idle CPU: storage or NFS hang. wchan shows where; fix the disk, a kill -9 will not help.
  • A growing pile of Z zombies: the parent never calls wait(). Each costs a PID and a PCB, not memory; at the PID limit (/proc/sys/kernel/pid_max, often 32768 or 4M) fork fails with EAGAIN. Fix the parent, or kill it so init adopts and reaps the zombies. In Docker, running an app as PID 1 that does not reap children causes this; use --init or tini.

Everyday analogy. A hospital patient chart: name, status, medication, where the patient is. The doctors (CPU) pick up charts, not patients.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking a zombie uses CPU or can be killed by kill -9 (it is already dead; only the parent reaping removes it).
  • Confusing D with S: D ignores signals and counts in load average.

notes.title: fork and exec
notes.html:
Unix creates processes in two steps: fork() clones the current process, exec() replaces the clone's program with a new one.

  • fork() returns twice: the child gets 0, the parent gets the child's PID. Child has a copy of memory, same open files, same environment.
  • execve(path, argv, envp) throws away the address space and loads a new program; PID stays the same, file descriptors stay open unless marked close-on-exec.
  • wait()/waitpid() lets the parent collect the exit status.
import os
pid = os.fork()
if pid == 0:                      # child
    os.execvp("ls", ["ls", "-l"])  # becomes ls
else:                              # parent
    os.waitpid(pid, 0)             # reap, avoids zombie

Why two steps? The gap lets a shell set up redirection between them: after fork, the child does dup2(fd, 1) to point stdout at a file, then execs the command. That is how ls > out.txt and pipes work.

$ strace -f -e trace=clone,execve,wait4 sh -c 'ls >/dev/null'
clone(child_stack=NULL, flags=CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID|SIGCHLD) = 4201
[pid 4201] execve("/bin/ls", ["ls"], ...) = 0
wait4(-1, [{WIFEXITED(s) && WEXITSTATUS(s) == 0}], 0, NULL) = 4201

Modern libc fork is really the clone syscall. For spawning, posix_spawn and vfork avoid copying page tables; vfork suspends the parent until the child execs.

Industry examples. Redis BGSAVE forks, and the child writes the snapshot while the parent keeps serving. Android's Zygote preloads the framework once and forks for every app, so app start shares already-loaded classes.

Everyday analogy. Photocopy a form (fork), then white-out it and write a completely different one (exec).

Common interview traps.

  • Believing fork copies all memory immediately (see next section).
  • Forking a huge multithreaded process: only the calling thread survives in the child, other threads' locks may stay locked forever. Prefer posix_spawn or exec right away.

notes.title: Copy-on-write
notes.html:
After fork, parent and child share the same physical pages, marked read-only. Only when one of them writes does the kernel copy that single page. This makes fork fast even for gigabytes of memory.

Mechanism: fork copies the page tables (not the data) and marks every writable page read-only in both. A write triggers a page fault; the fault handler sees "COW page", allocates a new frame, copies 4 KB, maps it writable for the writer, and resumes.

Worked example. Redis with 20 GB of data forks for a snapshot. Fork itself copies about 40 MB of page tables (20 GB / 4 KB pages x 8 bytes) and takes tens of ms (longer in VMs; Redis exposes latest_fork_usec). If the parent then updates 10% of pages during the 60 s snapshot, about 2 GB of extra RAM is needed. Machines with only 22 GB RAM would be OOM-killed. Rule of thumb: leave headroom, or set vm.overcommit_memory=1 as Redis docs advise so fork is not refused.

Transparent Huge Pages hurt here: one write copies 2 MB instead of 4 KB, causing latency spikes and RAM blow-up; Redis recommends disabling THP.

# Is memory shared? Look at Shared_Clean/Private_Dirty per mapping
grep -E 'Rss|Pss|Private_Dirty' /proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup

PSS (proportional set size) splits shared pages fairly among sharers: the honest per-process memory figure.

Everyday analogy. Two students share one textbook. The moment one wants to scribble in it, they photocopy only that page for themselves.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "fork duplicates memory": the correct answer is page tables plus COW.
  • Forgetting COW is also why exec right after fork is cheap: nothing was copied.

notes.title: Threads
notes.html:
A thread is a unit of execution inside a process. Threads of one process share the address space and file descriptors but each has its own stack, registers and program counter.

Shared: heap, globals, code, open files. Private: stack (default 8 MB virtual on Linux main thread; Java threads default to about 1 MB), registers, thread-local storage, signal mask.

In Linux a thread is just a task created with clone(CLONE_VM | CLONE_FILES | CLONE_FS | CLONE_SIGHAND | CLONE_THREAD...); the kernel schedules threads, not processes. ps -L, top -H and /proc/<pid>/task/ list them.

Process Thread
Memory Private Shared with siblings
Creation cost Higher (page tables) Lower (about 10 to 50 microseconds)
Communication IPC needed Direct memory (with locks)
Crash Isolated Takes down the whole process

Decision gravity. Threads are fast to talk to each other but any bug (data race, segfault) hits every thread. Processes isolate failures at the cost of IPC. Chosen per component; process-to-thread migration of a codebase is a large, hard-to-reverse rewrite.

Industry examples. Tomcat/Spring use a thread pool (default 200 threads). Node.js runs JS on one thread plus a libuv worker pool of 4. Go multiplexes goroutines (2 KB starting stacks) over few OS threads.

Everyday analogy. Workers in one kitchen sharing the same fridge. Faster to hand things over, but one person dropping the pan hurts everyone.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying threads are "lightweight processes" without mentioning shared address space.
  • Forgetting that one thread's uncaught segfault kills the whole process.

notes.title: Thread models
notes.html:
How user-level threads map to kernel threads decides cost and parallelism.

  • 1:1 (kernel threads): every language thread is an OS thread. Used by Linux pthreads, Java platform threads, Rust std::thread. True parallelism, kernel schedules everything. Cost: memory per thread (stack plus kernel structures, roughly 1 to 2 MB virtual, less resident) and context switch cost; a few thousand threads is the practical limit.
  • N:1 (green threads): many user threads on one OS thread. Cheap, but no multicore and one blocking syscall stalls all. Old Java "green threads", early Ruby.
  • M:N (hybrid): many user-level tasks scheduled onto a small pool of OS threads. Go goroutines, Erlang processes (WhatsApp: millions per node), Java 21 virtual threads, Kotlin coroutines.

Worked example. A server with 10,000 concurrent connections: thread-per-connection with 1 MB stacks is 10 GB virtual and heavy scheduler load. With an event loop (epoll plus a handful of threads) or virtual threads it is a few hundred MB. That is the C10K problem and why Nginx, Netty and Go replaced thread-per-request in high-connection servers.

Android link. Main (UI) thread must never block; blocking work goes to a pool or coroutine dispatcher (Dispatchers.IO is a pool of up to 64 threads by default). Coroutines are M:N in spirit.

Production signs. Thread leak: Threads: in /proc/<pid>/status or ps -o nlwp grows until pthread_create fails with EAGAIN ("unable to create new native thread" in Java). Check ulimit -u, /proc/sys/kernel/threads-max, cgroup pids.max.

Everyday analogy. Waiters (OS threads) each serving many tables (tasks), instead of hiring one waiter per table.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Go uses green threads on one core. It is M:N across all cores (GOMAXPROCS).
  • Forgetting that a blocking call on an M:N runtime may pin an OS thread.

notes.title: Context switch cost
notes.html:
A context switch is the CPU stopping one thread and starting another. Steps: save registers of the old task into its PCB, pick the next task, load its registers, switch the page table (if different process), resume.

Direct cost is roughly 1 to 5 microseconds (kernel work, register save). Indirect cost is often bigger: the new task finds cold CPU caches and, after a process switch, a flushed or partly invalid TLB (PCID helps). Thread switch inside one process is cheaper as the address space stays the same.

Types: voluntary (task blocked on I/O or a lock) and involuntary (its time slice ended or a higher priority task woke).

# Per-task counters
grep ctxt /proc/<pid>/status
voluntary_ctxt_switches:    81234
nonvoluntary_ctxt_switches: 1520

pidstat -w 1       # cswch/s (voluntary), nvcswch/s (involuntary)
vmstat 1           # 'cs' column = system-wide switches/s
perf stat -e context-switches,cpu-migrations ./app
$ pidstat -w 1
11:20:01  UID  PID   cswch/s nvcswch/s  Command
11:20:02  1000 4410  12000.00    35.00  java

Reading: high voluntary rate means lots of blocking (locks, small I/O, chatty RPC). High involuntary rate with a long run queue (r in vmstat larger than cores) means CPU oversubscription: too many runnable threads.

Worked example. 20,000 switches/s per core x 5 microseconds = 10% of one core gone, plus cache misses. A thread pool of 2,000 threads on 8 cores spending time in lock handoff is a classic cause of high sy and low throughput; cutting to about 16 to 32 threads (CPU-bound) often raises throughput. For I/O-bound work size is roughly cores x (1 + wait/compute).

Industry examples. LMAX Disruptor and Seastar (ScyllaDB) pin one thread per core and avoid locks to eliminate switching; Nginx uses one worker per core.

Everyday analogy. Putting down one jigsaw and starting another: time lost saving your place and re-finding pieces, worse each time the table is cluttered.

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting a single number as fact. Say it depends on CPU and kernel, and name how to measure (perf, pidstat -w).
  • Ignoring the indirect cache and TLB cost.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Process = running program with private address space, file descriptors and credentials; the PCB (task_struct) tracks it.
  • States R, S, D, T, Z; many D points to storage, many Z to a parent that does not wait().
  • fork clones, exec replaces; the gap enables redirection and pipes. Prefer posix_spawn from big multithreaded parents.
  • Copy-on-write makes fork cheap; Redis BGSAVE shows the memory spike when parents keep writing, and THP makes it worse.
  • Threads share memory and fds, have private stacks; Linux threads are clone tasks seen with top -H.
  • Models: 1:1, N:1, M:N; high connection counts favour event loops or M:N runtimes.
  • Context switch costs 1 to 5 microseconds directly, more through cold caches; measure with pidstat -w, vmstat cs, size pools to cores.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a program, a process and a thread? What does a process own?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Baseline vocabulary. Wrong answers here make every later answer unreliable.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A program is a file on disk: instructions and data. A process is a running instance of it with its own virtual address space, open file descriptors, credentials, environment and signal handlers. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process: threads share the address space and fds, but each has its own stack, registers and program counter. Run one program twice and you get two processes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Process
 |- Address space: code | data | heap | stack(s) | mapped libs
 |- File descriptors: 0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr, sockets, files
 |- Credentials, cwd, env, signal handlers
 |- Threads: each with own stack + registers

The isolation boundary is the process: one process cannot read another's memory without OS help (shared memory, ptrace, pipes). You can inspect it in /proc/PID:

ls /proc/$$                                   # cmdline cwd environ exe fd maps status task
grep -E 'Name|State|Pid|PPid|Threads|VmRSS' /proc/$$/status
ls -l /proc/$$/fd

Examples: Chrome uses a process per tab for isolation; Nginx a few worker processes each with epoll; Postgres process-per-connection; MySQL thread-per-connection.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using process and program interchangeably.
  • Calling threads "lightweight processes" without saying they share an address space.
  • Forgetting that fds are per-process (threads share the table, fork copies it).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What do threads not share? -> Stack, registers, thread-local storage, signal mask.
  2. Where do I see the thread count? -> Threads: in /proc/PID/status, ps -L, top -H.
  3. How does a process see only its own memory? -> Per-process page tables map virtual to physical addresses; the MMU enforces it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average gives textbook definitions. Senior links to failure domains: a crash in a thread kills the process; a crash in a process (tab, worker) is contained. They also say which one to choose per component.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Postgres cluster at 500 direct connections used 3 to 5 GB of private memory before running queries; adding PgBouncer fixed memory and context switching.

questions.subtopic: Process states, zombies and D state
questions.promptHtml: What process states does Linux show in ps, and what do a zombie and a D-state process mean?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Direct signal for debugging high load and PID leaks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: R running or runnable, S interruptible sleep, D uninterruptible sleep (usually blocked on disk or NFS, ignores signals), T stopped, Z zombie. A zombie has exited but its parent has not called wait(), so only its PCB and PID remain; it uses no CPU and kill -9 cannot remove it. A D process counts toward load average and cannot be killed until the I/O returns.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The kernel keeps a Process Control Block, struct task_struct in Linux: PID, state, saved registers, page table pointer, open files, signal state, scheduling info (priority, vruntime), parent and children, cgroup and namespace links.

New -> Runnable <-> Running -> Sleeping -> Runnable
                      Running -> Zombie -> (parent wait()) -> gone
$ ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,wchan:20,cmd
 2210  2188 D    io_schedule          dd if=/dev/sda of=/dev/null
 2301  1200 Z    -                    [worker] <defunct>
  • D: wchan shows where it waits. Fix the disk or NFS, not the process.
  • Z: fix the parent so it calls wait/waitpid (or ignores SIGCHLD). Killing the parent makes init adopt and reap the zombies.
  • Zombies cost a PID and a small PCB; the danger is exhausting pid_max (fork fails with EAGAIN).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Trying kill -9 on zombies or D processes.
  • Assuming a zombie uses memory or CPU.
  • Ignoring D states when load average is high but CPU idle.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does D exist? -> Some kernel code paths cannot safely be interrupted mid-operation (for example waiting for a disk transfer to a buffer).
  2. Zombie vs orphan? -> Orphan: parent died, adopted by init and reaped. Zombie: child dead, parent alive but not waiting.
  3. Docker container running your app as PID 1 accumulates zombies. Why? -> PID 1 must reap adopted orphans, and most apps do not; use --init or tini.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists states. Senior ties each to a symptom (high load with idle CPU means D; PID exhaustion means unreaped zombies) and the right fix.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A CI runner failed with "fork: Resource temporarily unavailable" because thousands of unreaped child shells exhausted the PID limit.

questions.promptHtml: How does Unix create a new process? Why are fork and exec separate calls?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the core Unix design idea and how shells implement redirection and pipes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: fork() clones the calling process: the child gets a copy of the address space, fds and environment, and fork returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent. execve() replaces the child's program with a new one; the PID stays and fds stay open unless marked close-on-exec. The parent calls wait() to collect the exit status. They are separate so the child can rearrange its fds between the two, which is how ls > out.txt and pipes work.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
import os
pid = os.fork()
if pid == 0:                          # child
    fd = os.open("out.txt", os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_TRUNC, 0o644)
    os.dup2(fd, 1)                    # stdout -> file, between fork and exec
    os.execvp("ls", ["ls", "-l"])
else:
    os.waitpid(pid, 0)                # reap, avoids zombie
Shell -> fork -> child shell -> dup2/close/chdir -> exec ls
Shell -> wait

Modern libc fork is the clone syscall. vfork and posix_spawn avoid copying page tables and are preferred when you only want to exec. Redis BGSAVE forks to snapshot; Android's Zygote preloads the framework then forks for each app.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing fork copies all memory eagerly (it is copy-on-write).
  • Forking a big multithreaded process: only the calling thread exists in the child, and locks held by other threads stay locked forever.
  • Forgetting wait, creating zombies.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does exec keep? -> PID, open fds without CLOEXEC, environment as passed, current directory.
  2. Why close-on-exec? -> To avoid leaking fds (sockets, secrets) into spawned programs.
  3. How does a | b work? -> Shell creates a pipe, forks twice, each child dup2s the pipe end to stdout or stdin, then execs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average describes the two calls. Senior explains why the gap exists, the CLOEXEC leak, and when to use posix_spawn.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A server leaked its listening socket into spawned helpers (no CLOEXEC); after a restart the old port stayed bound by orphan helpers.

questions.contextHtml:
A containerised image-conversion service starts failing with fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable after about 3 days uptime. Pod restarts fix it for 3 days. Memory and CPU are normal (30% / 15%). Inside the pod:

$ ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,cmd | awk '$3 ~ /Z/' | wc -l
31872
$ ps -o pid,ppid,cmd -p 1
  PID  PPID CMD
    1     0 python app.py
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max
32768

The app spawns ffmpeg through subprocess.Popen(...) per job and checks the exit code with poll() only for jobs that time out. A teammate suspects a memory leak and wants to raise memory limits.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise memory" or "increase the pids limit". Neither addresses unreaped children.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the app call wait for every child? Is PID 1 our app or an init? Any shell wrappers spawning grandchildren?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart the pod on a schedule or when the zombie count passes a threshold, as a stopgap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) our code never calls wait for successful jobs; (b) grandchildren (from sh -c) re-parented to PID 1 and PID 1 does not reap them; (c) pids cgroup limit too low (secondary).
  4. How I'd verify each: Count Z states by parent (ps -eo ppid,stat | awk '$2~/Z/{c[$1]++}END{for(p in c)print p,c[p]}'); check whether the zombies' parent is PID 1 (grandchildren) or the app's own children; grep code for Popen without communicate()/wait().
  5. Root cause: A zombie is a dead child awaiting wait(). Each holds a PID slot, and the pids cgroup cap of 32768 is hit, so fork returns EAGAIN. No memory is used, which is why memory graphs were flat.
  6. Fix: Short-term: run an init as PID 1 (docker run --init, tini, or shareProcessNamespace plus pause). Long-term: always communicate() or wait() in a context manager:
with subprocess.Popen(cmd) as p:     # context manager waits on exit
    p.communicate(timeout=60)
  1. Prevention: Alert on Z count and pids.current / pids.max; lint rule banning bare Popen; integration test that spawns 10k jobs and checks the zombie count.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raise pids.max (just delays). tini adds a tiny process but is cheap. Not kill -9 zombies (already dead).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would killing the parent help? -> Yes, zombies are re-parented to init and reaped, but you lose the service.
  • Why no CPU or memory symptoms? -> Zombies hold only a PCB and PID.
  • What about SIGCHLD set to SIG_IGN? -> The kernel auto-reaps children, but you lose exit statuses.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A scheduler pod passed all tests for 2 days then failed at the PID cap. The cause was a shell wrapper whose grandchildren re-parented to PID 1.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames memory or raises limits.
  • Hire: finds zombies, explains wait, and uses an init process.
  • Strong hire: distinguishes children vs grandchildren, adds monitoring on PID usage and tests.

questions.promptHtml: Explain copy-on-write. Why is fork fast even for a 20 GB process, and what is the hidden cost?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests virtual memory understanding and the production implications (Redis, memory spikes).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: After fork, parent and child share the same physical pages, marked read-only. The kernel copies only page tables, not data. When either side writes, a page fault fires, the kernel allocates a new frame, copies that 4 KB, maps it writable for the writer, and resumes. So fork costs page-table copying, tens of milliseconds for 20 GB, but later writes cause page copies, so memory use grows with the write rate.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
before write:  parent PTE -> frame F (RO)    child PTE -> frame F (RO)
child writes:  fault -> alloc frame G -> copy F to G -> child PTE -> G (RW)

Numbers: 20 GB / 4 KB = 5.2M pages x 8 B per PTE = about 40 MB of page tables copied. If the parent dirties 10% of pages during a 60 s snapshot, about 2 GB of extra RAM is needed.

Transparent Huge Pages make this worse: one write copies 2 MB, causing latency spikes and RAM bloat, which is why Redis advises disabling THP.

grep -E 'Rss|Pss|Private_Dirty|Shared_Clean' /proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup

PSS divides shared pages among sharers and is the honest per-process memory figure; RSS double counts shared pages.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Fork duplicates memory."
  • Sizing RAM for the parent only; the child can add up to the dirtied fraction.
  • Forgetting that fork itself stalls the parent (page-table copy, longer in VMs).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is exec right after fork cheap? -> Nothing was copied; the address space is discarded.
  2. What does vm.overcommit_memory=1 do for Redis? -> Lets fork succeed without the kernel refusing based on a worst-case commit estimate.
  3. How do you watch fork latency? -> Redis latest_fork_usec, or perf trace -e clone.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "pages are shared until written". Senior quantifies page-table cost and worst-case RAM, mentions THP and PSS, and plans headroom.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Redis node on 22 GB RAM with 20 GB data was OOM-killed during snapshot under heavy writes; the fix was more RAM headroom and THP off.

questions.promptHtml: What do threads share and not share, how are they implemented in Linux, and when would you choose processes over threads?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests mechanism knowledge and architectural judgment on isolation vs speed.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Threads share the heap, globals, code and open files; each has its own stack, registers, thread-local storage and signal mask. In Linux a thread is just a task created with clone(CLONE_VM | CLONE_FILES | CLONE_FS | CLONE_SIGHAND | CLONE_THREAD), and the kernel schedules threads, not processes. I choose threads for cheap sharing and communication, and processes for fault isolation and security boundaries, because a segfault or data race in one thread takes down the whole process.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Process Thread
Memory Private Shared with siblings
Creation Higher (page tables) Lower (about 10 to 50 microseconds)
Communication IPC (pipes, sockets, shm) Direct memory (needs locks)
Crash Isolated Takes down the process

Stack sizes: main thread usually 8 MB virtual, Java threads about 1 MB by default. Only touched stack pages become resident. ps -L, top -H, /proc/PID/task/ list threads.

Examples: Tomcat thread pool (default 200), Node.js one JS thread plus libuv pool of 4, Go goroutines on few OS threads.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Threads are lightweight processes" with no mention of the shared address space.
  • Forgetting one thread's uncaught fault kills everyone.
  • Sharing mutable state without synchronisation and blaming the OS.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does top show the same PID for many tasks? -> The thread group ID is the PID; each thread has its own TID. Use top -H.
  2. Which is easier to scale across machines? -> Processes with message passing; threads are bound to one address space.
  3. Why does Chrome use processes? -> Renderer compromise or crash is contained; sandboxing is per process.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average memorises the table. Senior speaks to blast radius, clone flags, and the cost of migrating between models.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A native image library crashed on a corrupt file; in the threaded server it killed all in-flight requests, so the team moved decoding into a worker process.

questions.contextHtml:
A Redis primary holds 20 GB on a 32 GB VM and snapshots every 15 minutes. Traffic is about to grow 10x in writes (from 5k to 50k writes/s, working set spread across all keys). Today INFO shows latest_fork_usec: 38000 and used_memory_peak: 20.3G. During the last snapshot the VM showed:

$ grep -E 'Private_Dirty|Rss' /proc/<redis-child>/smaps_rollup
Rss:            9437184 kB
Private_Dirty:  8650000 kB

A teammate says "the snapshot child uses 9 GB? Redis is leaking memory." The VM has THP enabled=always.
questions.promptHtml: Will the 10x load be safe? What do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more RAM" without understanding where the 9 GB came from, or "disable snapshots" without a durability trade-off.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is persistence required (RDB/AOF)? Do we have replicas that can snapshot instead? Is the key access pattern uniform? Is overcommit configured?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable THP now (echo never > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled), set vm.overcommit_memory=1, and move snapshotting to a replica.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) copy-on-write duplication of dirtied pages while parent serves writes (not a leak); (b) THP making each dirty page cost 2 MB; (c) real leak (unlikely, peak is stable at 20.3 GB).
  4. How I'd verify each: smaps_rollup on the child shows Private_Dirty, the dirtied copies; grep -i huge /proc/meminfo; compare memory before and after the child exits.
  5. Root cause: With fork, every page the parent writes during the snapshot is copied. Uniform writes at 50k/s over a 60 s snapshot touch millions of distinct pages; with THP each touch copies 2 MB. Worst case approaches the full dataset (20 GB more), exceeding 32 GB, so the OOM killer picks Redis.
  6. Fix: Short-term: THP off, replica takes snapshots, headroom to at least 1.6x the dataset. Long-term: shard to smaller instances (say 8 x 5 GB) so each fork is cheaper, or use AOF with rewrite scheduled off-peak.
  7. Prevention: Alert on latest_fork_usec, mem_fragmentation_ratio and RSS vs maxmemory; load test with realistic writes during snapshots.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Replica snapshots cost replication lag; more shards add client complexity. Not turn off persistence without agreeing the data-loss window.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fork now takes 38 ms; what at 100 GB? -> Page tables scale linearly (about 200 MB), so seconds in virtualised hosts; the parent stalls during that.
  • Would hugepages help fork speed? -> Fewer page-table entries, but copy granularity is worse.
  • Can memory sharing be seen per process? -> Use PSS, not RSS.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cache cluster ran fine for a year, then died every night at the same minute: snapshot time plus a nightly batch that rewrote 60% of keys.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: calls it a leak.
  • Hire: explains COW and disables THP, adds RAM or offloads snapshots.
  • Strong hire: quantifies worst case, tests under realistic write loads, plans sharding and alerts.

questions.contextHtml:
A Java service on Linux runs fine for hours, then fails with:

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread

while heap usage is only 35% and the container has 4 GB free. Metrics show the thread count climbing about 600 per hour.

$ ps -o nlwp= -p 3120
18204
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max
20000
$ jstack 3120 | grep -c 'pool-[0-9]*-thread-1'
5120

The code creates Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8) inside the request handler for some endpoints. A teammate wants to raise -Xmx because the error says OutOfMemoryError.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the error, find the cause, fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise the heap". The message mentions memory, but it is about OS thread limits, not the Java heap.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which limit trips first: pids.max, ulimit -u, threads-max, or virtual memory for stacks? Are pools created per request? Is there a shutdown path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart pods with rolling restarts before the count reaches the limit; temporarily lower -Xss or raise pids.max only to buy time.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) executors created per request and never shut down (fixed pool threads are non-daemon and live forever); (b) blocked threads accumulating (stuck on I/O); (c) a library creating threads per connection.
  4. How I'd verify each: jstack thread-name histogram (pool-N-thread-M with N growing means new pools); ls /proc/PID/task | wc -l over time; heap dump looking for ThreadPoolExecutor instances.
  5. Root cause: Each platform thread is an OS thread with a stack (1 MB virtual by default) and kernel structures. pthread_create fails with EAGAIN at the pids cgroup cap. Java reports that failure as OutOfMemoryError, which misleads.
  6. Fix: Short-term: create one shared pool at startup. Long-term: bounded pools, name threads, shut down on lifecycle end, consider virtual threads for blocking I/O.
private static final ExecutorService POOL = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
// handler: POOL.submit(task);   // never create a pool per request
  1. Prevention: Alert on thread count and pids.current/pids.max; static analysis flagging Executors.new* in request paths; load test for thread growth.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Raising limits hides the leak and shifts failure later. Unbounded cached pools can also explode under load.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would raising ulimit -u help? -> Only delays; the leak continues.
  • Why 18204 threads but memory is fine? -> Stacks are virtual and mostly untouched; the limit is a count, not RAM.
  • Would virtual threads remove this? -> They remove the OS-thread cap for blocking I/O but not leaked executors or unbounded work.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team saw this once a week on Monday mornings; the leak was in an admin endpoint used only by a weekly report.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases heap.
  • Hire: recognises thread-limit failure and finds the per-request pool.
  • Strong hire: checks all limit layers, adds monitoring and guards, and discusses virtual threads.

questions.promptHtml: Explain 1:1, N:1 and M:N thread models. Where do Java platform threads, goroutines and Kotlin coroutines sit, and what does a blocking call do in each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand how language runtimes map concurrency onto OS threads.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In 1:1 every language thread is an OS thread (pthreads, Java platform threads): real parallelism, but each costs a stack and kernel structures, so a few thousand is the practical ceiling. In N:1 many user threads share one OS thread: cheap, but no multicore, and one blocking syscall stalls everyone. M:N schedules many cheap tasks onto a small pool of OS threads: Go goroutines, Erlang processes, Java 21 virtual threads, Kotlin coroutines. The catch with M:N is a blocking call can pin an OS thread unless the runtime handles it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
M:N: goroutine 1 \
     goroutine 2  -> OS thread A -> core 1
     goroutine 3 -> OS thread B -> core 2
  • Go: goroutines start with about 2 KB stacks; the runtime parks goroutines blocked on network I/O (netpoller) and moves other goroutines onto the thread. A blocking syscall hands off the P (processor) so other goroutines run.
  • Java 21 virtual threads: unmounted when blocked on supported operations; pinned in some cases (synchronized blocks around blocking I/O in early versions; verify for your JDK).
  • Kotlin: Dispatchers.IO is a pool of up to 64 threads by default; blocking calls on Dispatchers.Default starve CPU-bound work.
  • Android: never block the main (UI) thread.

Example sizing: 10,000 connections as 1 MB stack threads is 10 GB virtual and heavy scheduling; an event loop or virtual threads need hundreds of MB.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Go uses green threads on one core." It is M:N across GOMAXPROCS cores.
  • Blocking calls in a coroutine dispatcher meant for CPU work.
  • Thinking virtual threads speed up CPU-bound code. They help with blocking I/O concurrency.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is the C10K problem? -> Serving 10k concurrent connections; thread-per-connection collapses, so event loops (epoll) and M:N runtimes are used.
  2. What happens when a goroutine makes a blocking syscall? -> Its OS thread blocks; the runtime detaches the P and runs other goroutines on another thread.
  3. When is 1:1 still the right choice? -> CPU-bound work with few tasks, native code that needs thread identity, simple debugging.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average names the models. Senior explains blocking semantics, pinning, and how to size pools and dispatchers.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Kotlin backend ran JDBC calls on Dispatchers.Default (cores-sized); a slow DB froze all request handling until they moved it to a bounded IO dispatcher.

questions.contextHtml:
A pricing service (8 cores, 2,000-thread pool in Tomcat after "we need more concurrency") hits 800 rps and p99 climbs to 1.8 s. Calls are CPU-heavy JSON plus a 3 ms cache lookup. pidstat -w 1 and vmstat 1:

11:20:02  UID  PID   cswch/s nvcswch/s  Command
11:20:02  1000 4410  12000.00  9500.00  java
 r  b   swpd   free   cache   in    cs  us sy id wa
60  0      0  812344 4123400 5100 45000  62 30  6  2

GC is normal (young GC 15 ms). top -H shows hundreds of threads at 1 to 2% each. Management asks to add 8 more cores.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, what do you change, and how do you size the pool?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add cores" or "tune GC". The CPU is busy doing the wrong work: switching.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How much of a request is CPU vs waiting? Is the pool shared between CPU and I/O work? What is the queue length and timeout policy?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce the pool to about 32 and cap the accept queue so excess load is rejected quickly instead of piling up.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) oversubscription: 60 runnable threads for 8 cores, high involuntary switches; (b) lock contention in the cache client (high voluntary switches); (c) GC (ruled out); (d) cold caches after every switch.
  4. How I'd verify each: pidstat -w -t splits voluntary and involuntary per thread: 9,500 involuntary means preemption by time slice; perf stat -e context-switches,cpu-migrations; jstack lock waits; a test varying pool size 16, 32, 64, 128 and plotting throughput.
  5. Root cause: r of 60 on 8 cores means 7 waiting runnable threads per core. Each switch costs 1 to 5 microseconds directly and more for cold L1/L2 and TLB, so about 20k switches/s per core consume 10% or more plus cache loss. Throughput falls as threads increase.
  6. Fix: Short-term: pool of 16 to 32 for CPU-bound work. For the I/O part, size as cores x (1 + wait/compute): 3 ms wait vs say 3 ms compute gives about 16. Long-term: separate pools for CPU and blocking I/O, async client for the cache, backpressure.
  7. Prevention: Dashboards for cs/s, r, thread count; load test every pool change; document the sizing formula.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A tiny pool plus slow downstream means queueing; add timeouts and shed load. Not add cores (the cost is per-switch, not capacity).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the work is mostly waiting on a remote service? -> Then more threads help, up to the formula; or switch to async/virtual threads.
  • What is the difference between voluntary and involuntary switches here? -> Voluntary: blocked on locks/I/O; involuntary: time slice expired or preempted.
  • Why does throughput drop rather than plateau? -> Cache and TLB thrash plus lock convoys make additional threads harmful.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team lowered a pool from 1,500 to 40 during an incident and p99 fell from seconds to 200 ms; they left the old setting in git history as a cautionary note.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds hardware.
  • Hire: identifies thread oversubscription from r, cs, nvcswch and reduces the pool.
  • Strong hire: sizes with a formula, separates pools, adds backpressure and guardrails.

questions.contextHtml:
You are designing a WebSocket gateway for a chat product: 200,000 concurrent mostly-idle connections per region, each sending a small message every 30 s on average, with occasional fan-out to 5,000 connections. The team knows Java and Kotlin; options:

  1. Thread-per-connection on Tomcat (platform threads, 1 MB stacks).
  2. Netty event loop with a small thread pool.
  3. Java 21 virtual threads with blocking-style code.
  4. Rewrite in Go.

Constraints: p99 delivery under 100 ms, 8-core nodes with 16 GB RAM, cost matters.
questions.promptHtml: Which model would you pick and why?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Go is faster" or "threads are fine, add nodes". It ignores memory per connection, scheduling, and the team's skills.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is any per-message work blocking (DB, remote calls)? Is the fan-out CPU-bound (serialisation)? Which JDK is approved? Ops maturity for new languages?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (Not an incident.) Prototype with a load generator at 50k then 200k connections to compare models.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) thread-per-connection: 200k x 1 MB virtual = 200 GB virtual, plus kernel structures; impossible on 16 GB at node scale; (b) Netty: tiny memory per connection (KBs), proven for this shape; (c) virtual threads: low memory, simpler code, but pinning and maturity risks; (d) Go: also fits but costs a rewrite.
  4. How I'd verify each: Measure per-connection memory (RSS / connections), p99 under fan-out bursts, GC pauses, and thread count (ps -o nlwp). Check pinning with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads.
  5. Root cause of the choice: Idle connections are the dominant cost. The OS thread model charges stack, scheduler entry and context switches per connection; event loops and M:N charge only per active event.
  6. Fix (recommendation): Netty (or a virtual-thread server if the JDK baseline allows) with epoll transport; fixed pool of about 8 to 16 event-loop threads; offload blocking work to a bounded pool; per-connection state in compact objects.
  7. Prevention: Soak tests at 1.5x, alerts on event-loop lag, a rule that event loop threads never block.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Event loops need discipline (no blocking) and are harder to debug; virtual threads give simpler code but newer failure modes. I would not rewrite in Go for a gain the JVM can match, unless the team wants that long-term.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fan-out to 5,000 connections blocks the loop for 20 ms; what now? -> Batch and shard fan-out across event loops, or offload serialisation.
  • Does epoll scale to 200k fds? -> Yes (O(ready)); raise ulimit -n and net.core.somaxconn.
  • What if a handler makes a blocking DB call? -> Dedicated bounded pool plus timeouts.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A gateway on thread-per-connection ran well at 5k connections and fell over at 20k during a promotion. The Netty rewrite held 150k on the same hardware.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: chooses by language preference.
  • Hire: rejects thread-per-connection for idle-heavy load, picks event loop or virtual threads.
  • Strong hire: quantifies memory, tests all options, defines event-loop rules, and plans for blocking work and fan-out.

questions.contextHtml:
A C++ server logs from many threads through a mutex-protected logger. To run a helper, a worker thread does a classic fork and then logs in the child before exec. About once per 5,000 helper launches, the child hangs forever; top shows the child stuck in S, 0% CPU, and the parent keeps waiting.

std::mutex g_log_mu;
void log(const std::string& s) { std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(g_log_mu); fputs(s.c_str(), stderr); }

void run_helper() {
    pid_t pid = fork();
    if (pid == 0) {
        log("child starting");          // BUG
        execlp("helper", "helper", nullptr);
        _exit(127);
    }
    int st; waitpid(pid, &st, 0);
}

cat /proc/<child>/stack is empty, strace -p <child> shows futex(0x55d0..., FUTEX_WAIT_PRIVATE, 2, NULL. It never reproduces in tests with one thread.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why it is rare, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a timeout on waitpid." That hides a deadlock.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many threads exist at fork time? Which locks (logger, malloc, stdio) might be held? Is the helper launch frequency tied to log volume?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Kill the stuck children after a watchdog timeout and alert; reduce logging in the launch path.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) another thread held g_log_mu (or the malloc/stdio lock) at the instant of fork; the child inherits the locked mutex but not the thread that would unlock it; (b) allocator lock held at fork (same class); (c) helper binary hangs (unlikely, the futex shows in the child before exec).
  4. How I'd verify each: The futex address in strace belongs to the logger mutex (gdb -p and print the address); reproduce by logging in a tight loop from 8 threads while forking; check info threads in the child (only one thread).
  5. Root cause: After fork in a multithreaded process, only the calling thread exists in the child, but all memory including mutex states is copied. A mutex locked by a thread that does not exist in the child is locked forever. Hence the rare, timing-dependent hang.
  6. Fix: In the child, call only async-signal-safe functions until exec (no logging, no malloc). Or avoid the hazard: use posix_spawn.
posix_spawnp(&pid, "helper", nullptr, nullptr, argv, environ);
  1. Prevention: Code review rule "nothing but dup2, close, exec, _exit between fork and exec"; stress test with many threads; consider pthread_atfork only as a last resort.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: pthread_atfork handlers are fragile. Not add sleep or retries. posix_spawn supports file actions but less custom setup than a hand-written child.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does Python's os.fork with threads warn in 3.12? -> Same hazard; the child may deadlock on inherited locks.
  • Is printf async-signal-safe? -> No; use write for emergency messages.
  • Does vfork help? -> The child shares the parent's memory and suspends the parent until exec; restrictions are even stricter.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A daemon hung roughly once a week at midnight when log rotation and a job launcher collided on the same lock.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds timeouts.
  • Hire: identifies inherited locked mutex and avoids logging in the child.
  • Strong hire: explains single-thread child semantics, proposes posix_spawn, and adds a stress test.

questions.contextHtml:
A PostgreSQL primary (64 GB RAM, 32 cores) serves a microservice fleet. Connections grew from 300 to 2,400 as services scaled out. Symptoms: query latency doubled, free shows 40 GB used by backends, and:

$ ps -eo pid,rss,cmd | grep 'postgres:' | wc -l
2417
$ vmstat 1
 r  b  free  cs     us sy id
48  0  3.1G  190000 55 30 14

Each backend is a separate process of 8 to 15 MB. Most connections are idle. You must introduce connection pooling without downtime; services use session features (some SET statements, a few prepared statements, advisory locks in two services).

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise max_connections" or "put PgBouncer in front tomorrow". The first worsens the problem, the second ignores session semantics.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which services use session state (SET, advisory locks, LISTEN, temp tables, prepared statements)? Pool mode needed? Is there a replica? What is the rollback plan?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap max_connections with headroom, kill idle-in-transaction sessions (idle_in_transaction_session_timeout), reduce per-service pool sizes now.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) process-per-connection memory and context switching (cs 190k/s, sy 30%); (b) idle connections holding memory and snapshots; (c) lock contention (no evidence).
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_stat_activity state counts; pidstat -w on postgres backends; smem/PSS for real memory (RSS double counts shared buffers); active vs idle ratio.
  5. Root cause: Postgres forks one process per connection; each carries private memory and counts in scheduling. 2,400 processes on 32 cores with mostly idle sessions waste memory and scheduler time while only about 40 are active.
  6. Fix (staged migration): Deploy PgBouncer in transaction mode for services without session state; keep session mode for the advisory-lock services. Move one low-risk service at a time by changing the connection string (feature flag), watch p99 and error rate, then roll on. Prepared statements: use protocol-level support in newer PgBouncer or disable server-side prepares in the driver. Target about 100 to 200 server connections.
  7. Prevention: Budget connections per service (pool size x replicas), alert on numbackends, load-test connection storms.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Transaction pooling breaks session state; extra hop adds a little latency; PgBouncer itself needs HA. Not raise max_connections (more processes, more contention).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not threads like MySQL? -> Process model is Postgres's architecture; changing is a large rewrite, so pool outside.
  • Active connections are 40; why choose 150? -> Headroom for bursts; test the knee in throughput.
  • Advisory locks with transaction pooling? -> Session-scoped locks break; use session mode or transaction-scoped advisory locks.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After moving to transaction pooling, one service started failing intermittently; it used SET search_path per session. A connection init hook fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises limits.
  • Hire: introduces pooling with a staged rollout.
  • Strong hire: handles session-state incompatibilities, sizes pools from active-connection data, and defines rollback and budgets.

questions.contextHtml:
A 24 GB-heap JVM service shells out to ffprobe for each uploaded file using ProcessBuilder. At 200 uploads/min p99 request latency has random 300 to 600 ms spikes, and perf trace shows:

clone(child_stack=NULL, flags=CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID|CLONE_CHILD_SETTID|SIGCHLD) = 8120 <0.412000>

The same call for a 100 MB process takes under 1 ms. Memory is at 85% of a 32 GB container, with vm.overcommit_memory=0. Occasionally spawns fail with Cannot allocate memory.
questions.promptHtml: Why is spawning slow and flaky and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ffprobe is slow." The slow part is the clone, before ffprobe even runs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: JDK version and launch mechanism (posix_spawn, vfork, or fork)? How big are page tables (heap size, THP)? Is ffprobe call frequency growing? Could we avoid a subprocess?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set jdk.lang.Process.launchMechanism=POSIX_SPAWN (or VFORK) if not already, and rate-limit concurrent spawns.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) fork copies page tables for 24 GB (about 48 MB), stalling the parent for hundreds of ms in a VM; (b) overcommit heuristics refuse the fork when RAM is tight (the ENOMEM); (c) GC threads contending (not shown).
  4. How I'd verify each: strace -T -e trace=clone,vfork or perf trace, correlate duration with heap size; try a small test JVM with a 24 GB -Xms (and -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch) to reproduce; grep -i Commit /proc/meminfo.
  5. Root cause: Even COW fork must copy page tables proportional to resident memory, and the kernel's commit accounting treats a fork as potentially doubling memory. Both scale with the parent's size, while the child immediately execs.
  6. Fix: Spawn without copying: posix_spawn/vfork. Better, move process launching into a small helper process (a sidecar or a pre-forked "spawner") that the JVM talks to over a pipe. Best, replace the subprocess with an in-process library (for example parse headers directly) if feasible.
  7. Prevention: Monitor clone latency, and keep a test with a large heap in CI for process launches; alert on ENOMEM from spawn.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A spawner adds a component to run and secure. vm.overcommit_memory=1 removes the refusal but shifts risk to the OOM killer. Not shrink the heap just to make fork cheap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does exec straight after fork still pay? -> The page-table copy happens before the exec.
  • Does THP help? -> Fewer PTEs, so a faster fork, but COW cost per write rises.
  • What does Android's Zygote do differently? -> Forks from a small preloaded process for sharing classes; the parent is not a giant heap.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A media service's tail latency vanished when the team swapped fork for a pre-started spawner holding 50 MB of RSS.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the external tool.
  • Hire: ties the stall to fork cost with a large heap, and switches to posix_spawn/vfork.
  • Strong hire: explains page-table and commit-accounting effects, offers a spawner or in-process alternative, and monitors it.
